clue.text: Writer gets fish without bread

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the fish wraps round the bread

parts.note: the tope is a small shark, a kind of fish
a roll is a small loaf of bread

explanation.surface: An author goes hungry, catching fish but having no bread to go with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside here, not lacking: ROLL goes inside TOPE. The OCR text dropped 'fish', which the page prints.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire books.

clue.text: Officer upset mine employees

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down clue the word for mine is read upwards

parts.note: a pit is a mine
staff are the employees

explanation.surface: An official overturned the miners' working conditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reverses PIT to TIP. A tipstaff is a court officer, named for the metal-tipped staff he carried.
explanation.definitionFit: A tipstaff is a sheriff's or court official who carries a tipped staff of office.

clue.text: Working for entertainment, gets into muddle

parts.note: an opera is a stage entertainment

indicators.note: muddle shows the letters of the short word are jumbled

explanation.surface: Performing to amuse people lands someone in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muddle' rearranges INTO to TION. 'In operation' means working.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine in operation is functioning, so the noun fits the sense of running.

clue.text: Catalogues in which charges appeared ?

explanation.surface: Records that note what costs were made.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'charges' are knights' charges: the lists were the enclosed ground where jousts were held.
explanation.definitionFit: Lists are catalogues, and the lists were the barriers round a tilting ground where knights charged.

clue.text: Hit Evoe, once

parts.note: Evoe was the pen name of E. V. Knox, so he stood for the magazine Punch, which he edited
once means former, so ED stands for the editor he used to be

explanation.surface: A man known as Evoe was struck at one time.
explanation.walkthrough: E. V. Knox, 'Evoe', edited Punch, the British humour magazine, from 1932 to 1949: he was once Punch's editor, PUNCH ED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be punched is to be hit with a fist.

clue.text: Gives vent to rage, and dies?

explanation.surface: Someone flies into a fury and then expires.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second sense: dies are the tools that press a design into metal, and so are stamps.
explanation.definitionFit: An angry person stamps their feet; a stamp is also a die, the block used to impress a design.

clue.text: Weapons for a private army, perhaps

definitions.text: Weapons for a private army, perhaps

parts.words: Weapons for a private army, perhaps
parts.note: a private soldier is nicknamed Tommy, so guns for him, though the gun was famed among gangsters' private armies

explanation.surface: Arms supplied to a militia raised by an individual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' is a soldier's rank: Tommy Atkins is the British private. A private army is also a gang, and gangsters carried the Thompson submachine gun.
explanation.definitionFit: The tommy gun is the Thompson submachine gun of the 1920s gang era.

clue.text: Fruit order expelling Adam?

parts.note: Adam was the first man
go is the order that sends someone out

explanation.surface: A command throwing Adam out over a piece of fruit, as in Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the forbidden fruit: the order expelling Adam is 'Man, go!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mango is a sweet tropical stone fruit.

clue.text: Rough set ask cook for meat

indicators.note: rough means roughly handled, so the letters of the two words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A coarse group asks someone to cook their meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rough' rearranges SET and ASK; 'cook' supports it in the surface and reads as a second anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Steaks are thick slices of beef or other meat.

clue.text: Note added to charity — by David?

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the plural noun: works written by David

parts.note: PS, the postscript, is a note added to a letter
alms are gifts given in charity

explanation.surface: A postscript about charity, signed by David.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By David' stands for the songs written by David, the king traditionally credited with the Book of Psalms.
explanation.definitionFit: King David is the traditional author of the Old Testament songbook.

clue.text: Birds found by rustics including one of 15

indicators.note: including says the rustics hold the other piece inside them

parts.note: rustics are country people, peasants
15-down is ASPIRATES, and an aspirate is the letter H, the breathy sound

explanation.surface: Game birds are spotted by country folk out on the land.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference sends you to 15-down: an aspirate is an H sound, so one of them is the letter H.
explanation.definitionFit: Pheasants are long-tailed game birds shot in the countryside.

clue.text: Meat for a thousand Anglicans?

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
Anglicans are people in the CE, the Church of England, so the word gives IN plus CE

explanation.surface: A huge order of meat for a church gathering of a thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Anglicans' as those 'in C.E.', members of the Church of England; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Mince is minced meat, chopped finely.

clue.text: Vehicles for fashionable retired types

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word for fashionable is read backwards

parts.note: smart means fashionable

explanation.surface: Transport provided for stylish pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired types' looks like pensioners, but 'retired' tells you to turn SMART round; 'types' only rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Trams are passenger vehicles running on rails in the street.

clue.text: Plant shrub to get wine?

parts.note: holly is an evergreen shrub
hock is a German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: Someone puts a bush in the ground hoping it will yield wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb, but it is the definition. HOCK is the British name for Rhine white wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The hollyhock is a tall garden flower of the mallow family.

clue.text: Honest description of an old-fashioned blonde

explanation.surface: A truthful account of a fair-haired woman who is behind the times.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the phrase: FAIR describes a blonde, SQUARE an old-fashioned person, and the whole phrase means honest.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair and square means above board; fair hair is blonde and a square is someone conventional and out of date.

clue.text: Like Morgan and his men, they might be dropped

parts.note: as means like
Henry Morgan was a seventeenth-century buccaneer with a band of pirates

explanation.surface: Like a buccaneer's crew, they might be dropped overboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping your aitches means leaving out H sounds, the aspirates.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspirates are breathed H sounds, which careless speakers drop.

clue.text: See 14
Country where robots behead the fairy queen

parts.note: R.U.R. is Karel Capek's play about robots, which gave English the word

indicators.note: behead removes the first letter of the queen's name

parts.note: Titania is queen of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: A land where machines execute the fairy queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behead' takes T from TITANIA to leave ITANIA. Ruritania is the made-up kingdom of The Prisoner of Zenda.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the fictional Central European kingdom of Anthony Hope's novels.

clue.text: Being disloyal to poor Albert about agreement

indicators.note: about means going round, so the jumbled name surrounds the word for agreement
poor suggests something in bad shape, so the letters of the name are reshaped

parts.note: ay (aye) is a word of agreement, yes

explanation.surface: Treachery towards poor Albert over a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges ALBERT to BETRAL, and 'about' wraps it round AY: BETR-AY-AL.
explanation.definitionFit: Betrayal is treachery, the act of being false to someone who trusts you.

clue.text: Marksman gets bird to the right

parts.note: the snipe is a wading bird with a long bill
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A shooter bags a bird on his right-hand side.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits, since the word for a marksman comes from shooting snipe.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniper is a sharpshooter firing from hiding.

clue.text: Port given to little boy — created disturbance

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port
Ted is a short form of Edward, a boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone made a scene when a drink of port was given to a small child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink, but it is the harbour city RIO.
explanation.definitionFit: To riot is to create a violent public disturbance.

clue.text: Keep watch?

explanation.surface: An order to stand guard.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words: you keep a law or custom and you watch something closely, both senses of the one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe a rule is to keep it, and to observe a scene is to look at it.

clue.text: Eccentrics given their head? Just a bit

parts.note: odd men are eccentrics

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, here the word their

explanation.surface: Should oddballs be allowed free rein? Only slightly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Given their head' looks like 'allowed to run free', but it adds T, the head of 'their'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oddment is a leftover scrap, just a bit of something.

clue.text: Rustics put their vehicle aboard

indicators.note: put here means placed within, the cart going into the ship

parts.note: aboard means on a ship, SS being the steamship abbreviation
a wain is a farm wagon, the countryman's vehicle

explanation.surface: Country lads load their cart onto a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: WAIN is the old word for a farm wagon; it goes inside SS, steamship.
explanation.definitionFit: Swains are country youths, especially shepherd lovers in pastoral verse.

clue.text: River crossing the county

parts.note: a river is a stretch of water
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: A river ford leads across into the county.
explanation.walkthrough: WATERFORD is a county in the south-east of Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterford is an Irish county on the south coast.

clue.text: Material West found in drawer

indicators.note: found in says one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a till is a cash drawer

explanation.surface: Cloth from the West is discovered in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawer' is the cash drawer, TILL, not the furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Twill is a woven fabric with diagonal ribs.

clue.text: Writer for the old-fashioned family man

explanation.surface: An author who writes for the traditional father.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter Pater was a Victorian essayist; the Latin word for father was old schoolboy slang for one's dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter Pater was a Victorian critic, and 'pater' is dated British slang for a father.

clue.text: " A six years' darling of a —— size!" (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: A six years' darling of a —— size!" (Wordsworth)

parts.words: A six years' darling of a —— size!" (Wordsworth)
parts.note: fill the gap in the line from the Immortality Ode, an old spelling of a word for a tiny person

explanation.surface: A quotation from Wordsworth with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Wordsworth's Intimations of Immortality, describing a small child; PIGMY is an older spelling of pygmy.
explanation.definitionFit: A pygmy size is very small, as a six-year-old is.

clue.text: Macbeth's tale-teller, or the subject of Dostoievsky's

explanation.surface: Two literary questions: who narrates in Shakespeare's tragedy, and what is the Russian novel about?
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth calls life 'a tale told by an idiot'; Dostoevsky's novel is The Idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Macbeth's speech names a fool as the teller of life's tale, and Dostoevsky's novel takes Prince Myshkin, a holy fool, as its title figure.

clue.text: By derivation the exit to go out of

definitions.text: By derivation the exit to go out of

parts.words: By derivation the exit to go out of
parts.note: taken by its roots, the word is formed from the verb meaning to come out, so it names an exit to leave through; normally it means a crisis

explanation.surface: An etymology lesson about the meaning of a way out.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from 'emerge', to come out, so by derivation it is the way you go out; the emergency exit plays on this.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden crisis is the everyday sense, but the root is the Latin verb for rising out of water.

clue.text: Ostentation raises but weakens the spirits?

explanation.surface: Showing off cheers people up but leaves them feeling flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' is whisky, not mood: a splash of soda raises the level in the glass but dilutes the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a splash is a showy display, and a splash is a dash of water added to a drink.

clue.text: Hoisted by a yachtsman who wishes to remain at his moorings?

definitions.text: Hoisted by a yachtsman who wishes to remain at his moorings

parts.words: Hoisted by a yachtsman who wishes to remain at his moorings
parts.note: read the sail's name as an order to stay put, though it is a real sail set on a ship's stays

explanation.surface: A sailor hoists something to show he wants to stay moored.
explanation.walkthrough: A staysail is a sail set on a stay, a rope bracing the mast; the clue reads its name as 'stay' plus 'sail'.
explanation.definitionFit: A staysail is a triangular sail rigged on one of the stays that brace a mast.
